Act III: where they hit their limits. Four of them: judgment, measurement, containment, power.
So far you've seen the labs at their best; now the independent tests.

notes: Paul A. David, «The Dynamo and the Computer», American Economic Review, 1990.
In 1899 electric motors were under 5% of US factory drive power. Until about 1920 most factories added motors to the old shaft-and-belt system and kept the old layout.
Productivity jumped only in the 1920s, about 40 years after the first power station, once one motor per machine let factories be rebuilt around the flow of work.
His data's lesson: the gains came from redesigning the work, not from adding the motor.
David himself warns against pushing the analogy too far; say so if asked.
Cue: Value.

notes: Four contrasts, bolted on vs redesigned. No data on this slide: it's the approach.
Information moved by hand → information already there at the point of work.
People coordinating every step → AI executes; people handle judgment and exceptions.
Decisions after the fact → decisions inside the workflow. Training apart from the work → teams learn by operating the new system.
Optional (your observation): «Most LATAM organizations are optimizing instead of redesigning.»

approach.transition: Where do you start? Where checking is cheap.

notes: Our reading of tonight's evidence: AI leaps where results are cheap to check (code, proofs) and lags where checking needs judgment (Epoch's study; METR on “taste”).
In a business: reconciliations, forms, code; you can verify the output. These examples are ours.
Strategy, research, taste still need a person to judge.
Takeaway: choose work whose result you can verify, and build the check first; remember ZoomInfo's judge.
